Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed a well-defined, encapsulated lesion in the root of the tongue, measuring 63 × 40 × 45 mm. case_info.explanation: Schwannomas are rare tumors of the oral cavity, accounting for less than 1% of all head and neck neoplasms.1The tongue is one of the most common intraoral sites, typically involving the hypoglossal or lingual nerve. Tongue schwannomas represent a small fraction of benign peripheral nerve sheath tumors. They can occur at any age but are most frequently diagnosed in the third to fifth decades of life, with no significant sex predilection. These tumors are primarily slow growing and asymptomatic, often discovered incidentally or only once they grow large enough to cause mechanical obstruction or interfere with speech or swallowing. On examination, tongue schwannomas are usually submucosal and well-defined; however, assessment of texture, mobility, and fixation is important to differentiate them from more aggressive lesions.1-4 MRI plays a pivotal role in preoperative diagnosis and assessment; its superior soft tissue contrast allows for precise localization and detailed assessment of tumor size, location, and relationship to surrounding structures, which is essential for referral and surgical planning. Sagittal postcontrast T1-weighted MRI clearly delineated the craniocaudal extent and displacement of adjacent structures without evidence of invasion (Figure 2). On MRI, schwannomas typically appear as well-demarcated lesions that are hypointense on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on T2-weighted images. They often exhibit the split-fat sign, which refers to a rim of surrounding fat visible on T1-weighted imaging, an indicator of a well-encapsulated, slowly growing lesion.1,4,5Gadolinium-enhanced MRI shows schwannomas as bright lesions with heterogeneous enhancement, due to their cellular heterogeneity, which reflects varying degrees of vascularity and tissue density.4,6MRI is crucial in differentiating schwannomas from malignant tumors, such as squamous cell carcinoma (SCC). Differentiation of tongue schwannomas from malignant or other benign submucosal lesions is important. SCC is the most common tumor of the tongue. SCCs are aggressive tumors that commonly arise in this mucosa and will exhibit deep invasion.7SCCs of a similar magnitude most often have an appearance that is painful (otalgia), ulcerative, and highly aggressive with lymphatic spread. Common MRI findings suggest poorly defined, infiltrative borders and heterogeneous enhancement.4,7 Granular cell tumors are often mistaken for schwannomas, present as firm submucosal nodules, and show moderate enhancement on MRI but lack the T2 hyperintensity and fascicular architecture of schwannomas. Histopathology remains essential for differentiation.2,3,7 Salivary gland tumors arising from minor salivary glands are typically submucosal in location and may be benign or malignant. They appear well defined with smooth, pushing borders with cystic changes and moderate enhancement patterns on MRI.6,7Lipomas are benign fatty tumors that are soft to the touch, appear hyperintense on T1-weighted imaging, and lack gadolinium enhancement due to fat content, differentiating them from schwannomas.1,5,7 The clinical course of tongue schwannomas is typically indolent, with slow progression over months or years. This female patient experienced fullness and roughness for nearly 4 months before presentation. Schwannomas are encapsulated, allowing for successful enucleation with minimal risk of recurrence.1-4,8She underwent surgical excision at a tertiary center. Complete surgical excision remains the standard of care. Postoperative histopathological examination of the excised tumor, essential to rule out a malignant tumor, confirmed schwannoma. Schwannomas, particularly long-standing lesions, may demonstrate degenerative features, such as cystic change, nuclear atypia, and calcification termedancient change,which can mimic malignant tumors and require careful histologic interpretation2,3,9The patient recovered well postoperatively, with no evidence of recurrence or functional impairment. MRI remains the imaging modality of choice for preoperative planning and postoperative monitoring. Although schwannomas and malignant tumors may both exhibit restricted diffusion on diffusion-weighted imaging, schwannomas demonstrate higher mean apparent diffusion coefficient values due to their heterogeneous cellular and myxoid architecture.5,10Integration of diffusion-weighted imaging with conventional MRI features, such as well-defined encapsulation, enhances differentiation between these entities. This case report highlights the importance of thorough clinical and radiological evaluation, particularly MRI sequences, in the assessment of patients with submucosal tongue lesions. Tongue schwannomas, though rare, should be considered in the diagnosis and differentiated from malignant or other benign lesions. Adequate radiological assessment and histopathological confirmation are essential to ensure accurate diagnosis and optimal patient outcomes.

case_info.explanation: Schwannomas are rare tumors of the oral cavity, accounting for less than 1% of all head and neck neoplasms.1The tongue is one of the most common intraoral sites, typically involving the hypoglossal or lingual nerve. Tongue schwannomas represent a small fraction of benign peripheral nerve sheath tumors. They can occur at any age but are most frequently diagnosed in the third to fifth decades of life, with no significant sex predilection. These tumors are primarily slow growing and asymptomatic, often discovered incidentally or only once they grow large enough to cause mechanical obstruction or interfere with speech or swallowing. On examination, tongue schwannomas are usually submucosal and well-defined; however, assessment of texture, mobility, and fixation is important to differentiate them from more aggressive lesions.1-4 MRI plays a pivotal role in preoperative diagnosis and assessment; its superior soft tissue contrast allows for precise localization and detailed assessment of tumor size, location, and relationship to surrounding structures, which is essential for referral and surgical planning. Sagittal postcontrast T1-weighted MRI clearly delineated the craniocaudal extent and displacement of adjacent structures without evidence of invasion (Figure 2). On MRI, schwannomas typically appear as well-demarcated lesions that are hypointense on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on T2-weighted images. They often exhibit the split-fat sign, which refers to a rim of surrounding fat visible on T1-weighted imaging, an indicator of a well-encapsulated, slowly growing lesion.1,4,5Gadolinium-enhanced MRI shows schwannomas as bright lesions with heterogeneous enhancement, due to their cellular heterogeneity, which reflects varying degrees of vascularity and tissue density.4,6MRI is crucial in differentiating schwannomas from malignant tumors, such as squamous cell carcinoma (SCC). Differentiation of tongue schwannomas from malignant or other benign submucosal lesions is important. SCC is the most common tumor of the tongue. SCCs are aggressive tumors that commonly arise in this mucosa and will exhibit deep invasion.7SCCs of a similar magnitude most often have an appearance that is painful (otalgia), ulcerative, and highly aggressive with lymphatic spread. Common MRI findings suggest poorly defined, infiltrative borders and heterogeneous enhancement.4,7 Granular cell tumors are often mistaken for schwannomas, present as firm submucosal nodules, and show moderate enhancement on MRI but lack the T2 hyperintensity and fascicular architecture of schwannomas. Histopathology remains essential for differentiation.2,3,7 Salivary gland tumors arising from minor salivary glands are typically submucosal in location and may be benign or malignant. They appear well defined with smooth, pushing borders with cystic changes and moderate enhancement patterns on MRI.6,7Lipomas are benign fatty tumors that are soft to the touch, appear hyperintense on T1-weighted imaging, and lack gadolinium enhancement due to fat content, differentiating them from schwannomas.1,5,7 The clinical course of tongue schwannomas is typically indolent, with slow progression over months or years. This female patient experienced fullness and roughness for nearly 4 months before presentation. Schwannomas are encapsulated, allowing for successful enucleation with minimal risk of recurrence.1-4,8She underwent surgical excision at a tertiary center. Complete surgical excision remains the standard of care. Postoperative histopathological examination of the excised tumor, essential to rule out a malignant tumor, confirmed schwannoma. Schwannomas, particularly long-standing lesions, may demonstrate degenerative features, such as cystic change, nuclear atypia, and calcification termedancient change,which can mimic malignant tumors and require careful histologic interpretation2,3,9The patient recovered well postoperatively, with no evidence of recurrence or functional impairment. MRI remains the imaging modality of choice for preoperative planning and postoperative monitoring. Although schwannomas and malignant tumors may both exhibit restricted diffusion on diffusion-weighted imaging, schwannomas demonstrate higher mean apparent diffusion coefficient values due to their heterogeneous cellular and myxoid architecture.5,10Integration of diffusion-weighted imaging with conventional MRI features, such as well-defined encapsulation, enhances differentiation between these entities. This case report highlights the importance of thorough clinical and radiological evaluation, particularly MRI sequences, in the assessment of patients with submucosal tongue lesions. Tongue schwannomas, though rare, should be considered in the diagnosis and differentiated from malignant or other benign lesions. Adequate radiological assessment and histopathological confirmation are essential to ensure accurate diagnosis and optimal patient outcomes.
